questions.prompt: State what it means for a square matrix A to have inverse \(A^{-1}\).
questions.answer: A square matrix A has inverse \(A^{-1}\) when multiplying them in either order gives the identity matrix. That means AA^{-1} = I and \(A^{-1}\)\(A=I\). The inverse reverses the linear effect of A.

questions.prompt: Verify that \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) is the inverse of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: Here A is the \(2\times 2\) identity matrix and B is also the \(2\times 2\) identity matrix. Multiplying identity matrices gives the identity matrix: \(AB\) = \(I_2\) and \(BA\) = \(I_2\). Therefore B is the inverse of A. In fact, the identity matrix is its own inverse.

questions.prompt: Use the \(2\times 2\) inverse formula to find the inverse of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: For a diagonal matrix, the inverse has reciprocal diagonal entries when the diagonal entries are non-zero. Since A scales the first coordinate by 2 and the second by 3, the inverse scales by 1/2 and 1/3. Therefore \(A^{-1}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\0&1/3\end{pmatrix}\).

For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), the inverse is (1/(ad - bc))\(\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}\) when ad - bc is non-zero. Here ad - \(bc=1\)*4 - \(2\cdot3\) = 4 - 6 = -2. Therefore \(A^{-1}\) = (-1/2)\(\begin{pmatrix}4&-2\\-3&1\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\3/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix}\).

For a \(2\times 2\) matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), invertibility requires ad - bc not equal to 0. Here ad - \(bc=2\)*2 - \(4\cdot1\) = 4 - 4 = 0. Since the determinant is 0, A is not invertible.

Multiply the matrices. First product: \(\begin{pmatrix}2\cdot 1 + 1\cdot (-1)&2\cdot (-1) + 1\cdot 2\\1\cdot 1 + 1\cdot (-1)&1\cdot (-1) + 1\cdot 2\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). Since both matrices are square and this product is \(I_2\), checking the reverse product also gives \(I_2\): \(\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot 2 + (-1)\cdot 1&1\cdot 1 + (-1)\cdot 1\\(-1)\cdot 2 + 2\cdot 1&(-1)\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 1\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). Therefore the matrices are inverses.

If \(Ax=b\) and A is invertible, then x = \(A^{-1}\)b. Multiply \(A^{-1}\) by b: \(\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\)\(\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot 3 + (-1)\cdot 1\\(-1)\cdot 3 + 2\cdot 1\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). Therefore x = \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: Find all real t such that \(A=\begin{pmatrix}t&1\\4&2\end{pmatrix}\) is not invertible.
questions.answer: A \(2\times 2\) matrix is not invertible when ad - \(bc=0\). Here ad - \(bc=t\)*2 - \(1\cdot4\) = 2t - 4. Set this equal to 0: 2t - 4 = 0. Then 2t = 4, so \(t=2\). Therefore A is not invertible only when \(t=2\).

questions.prompt: A student says every non-zero matrix has an inverse. Disprove this using \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: The matrix A is not the zero matrix because it has non-zero entries. However, its determinant is \(1\cdot4\) - \(2\cdot2\) = 4 - 4 = 0. A \(2\times 2\) matrix with determinant 0 is not invertible. Therefore this non-zero matrix does not have an inverse, so the student's claim is false.

questions.prompt: If A and B are invertible square matrices of the same size, explain why (\(AB\))^{-1} = \(B^{-1}\)\(A^{-1}\) rather than \(A^{-1}\)\(B^{-1}\).
questions.answer: To undo the product \(AB\), operations must be reversed. Check \(B^{-1}\)\(A^{-1}\): (\(AB\))(\(B^{-1}\)\(A^{-1}\)) = A(BB^{-1})\(A^{-1}\) = AIA^{-1} = AA^{-1} = I. Also (\(B^{-1}\)\(A^{-1}\))(\(AB\)) = \(B^{-1}\)(\(A^{-1}\)A)\(B=B^{-1}\)IB = \(B^{-1}\)\(B=I\). Therefore \(B^{-1}\)\(A^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(AB\). The order must reverse because matrix multiplication is not commutative.
